Start with cold-air drainage. Cold air is denser than warm air, so on a clear, calm night it flows downhill like water and pools in valley bottoms, hollows, and any depression. This katabatic drainage produces a genuine temperature inversion, and the difference between a valley floor and a bench thirty metres above it is commonly 5 to 10°C, occasionally more. A site partway up a gentle slope can therefore be dramatically warmer than the flat, inviting hollow just below it. The trade-off runs the other way at the top: exposed ridgelines and summits escape the cold sink but take the full wind, which usually costs more than the inversion gains. The sweet spot is a bench or terrace on the hillside, out of both the pool and the worst of the wind. In the northern hemisphere a south or south-east-facing aspect also catches morning sun, which matters more than it sounds when you are cold at dawn.

Always look up before committing. Dead branches hanging in the canopy and dead or leaning trees, known as widow-makers, fall without warning, and they fall most readily in wind or after rain loosens root systems. People have been killed sleeping under one. Scan the full circle of trees whose height could reach your site, not just the one directly overhead.

Water is a real trade-off rather than a simple positive. Being near a stream means easy access for drinking and washing, and it also means more insects, colder and damper air overnight in the immediate channel, and background noise that masks approaching weather or people. In arid terrain it becomes an outright hazard: dry washes and canyon bottoms flash flood from rain falling many miles upstream that you never see or hear, and a flat, clear, gravel-floored wash is one of the most dangerous places to sleep in that country precisely because it looks like the best campsite available. A working compromise is to camp roughly sixty metres back from and above the water.

Finish with three quick checks. Note the prevailing wind and orient the entrance away from it, using the lean of trees and the shape of drifted snow or debris as evidence rather than relying on the moment's breeze. Look at the ground itself for game trails, since animals will walk their route through your camp at night, and for ant nests, wasp holes, and standing deadwood. And in winter mountains, check what is above you on the slope: never build beneath an avalanche path, a cornice, or a gully that funnels snow, however sheltered the spot appears.

sections.heading: Snow Shelters: The Quinzhee and the Trench
sections.body:
Snow feels like the enemy of warmth, and a well-built snow shelter is among the best-insulated structures buildable by hand. The reason is that snow is mostly trapped air. Low-density snow conducts heat at roughly 0.05 to 0.15 watts per metre per kelvin, comparable to commercial building insulation and a fraction of the figure for ice or wet ground, so a wall of it is an excellent blanket rather than a block of cold.

A quinzhee is built by piling loose snow into a mound roughly seven to eight feet across and letting it sit undisturbed for at least an hour or two before hollowing it out. That waiting period is not optional. It allows sintering, in which the contact points between snow crystals partly melt under the mound's own weight and then refreeze, bonding the pile into a self-supporting dome. Mixing snow of different temperatures and grain sizes as you shovel accelerates it. Before digging, push a couple of dozen sticks about a foot long through the outer surface, aimed radially toward the centre. When you meet the inner tip of a stick while hollowing, stop digging at that point, which leaves a wall roughly twelve inches thick without the risk of breaking through. Raise a sleeping platform above the entrance level so cold air drains down and out, which is the same trick that makes a proper snow cave warm.

A snow trench is the low-effort alternative and needs perhaps thirty minutes: dig body-width and as deep as the pack allows, roof it with branches, skis, a tarp, or cut snow blocks, and shovel loose snow over the roof for extra insulation. Either shelter's interior tends to stabilise close to 32°F (0°C) regardless of how much colder it gets outside, which in a −20°F night is a fifty-degree improvement bought with a shovel.

That same airtight insulating quality carries two genuine hazards, and both are worth treating as hard rules rather than judgment calls. Carbon dioxide from your own breathing accumulates in a sealed space, so a snow shelter needs a ventilation hole of at least fist size poked through the roof, checked periodically, since drifting snow and refreezing meltwater can seal it over during the night. Keep a shovel or a ski pole inside for exactly that reason, and for digging out if the entrance drifts shut. Running any flame or stove inside a poorly ventilated snow shelter risks lethal carbon monoxide accumulation, and it also melts the ceiling into a dripping glaze that then refreezes into ice, destroying the insulation.

The honest caveat is effort. Building a quinzhee is hard physical work, and soaking your layers in sweat while doing it can leave you worse off than before. Strip a layer, work slowly, and keep a dry set sealed in the pack for the moment you stop.

sections.heading: Recognizing Hypothermia Before It's an Emergency
sections.body:
Hypothermia, a fall in core body temperature below about 95°F (35°C), rarely announces itself clearly, and the person developing it is usually the last to notice, because impaired judgment is one of its earliest symptoms. That single fact reorganises the whole problem: recognition is a group responsibility, and the useful question is not how you feel but how the person next to you is behaving.

Wilderness medicine teaches a mnemonic for the mild stage, the umbles. Mumbles is slurred or slowed speech. Fumbles is clumsy hands, dropped items, and trouble with zippers, buckles, or knots, which appears early because manual dexterity degrades badly once hand temperature falls below roughly 60°F. Stumbles is unsteady walking and poor coordination. Grumbles is irritability, withdrawal, apathy, or an uncharacteristic refusal to keep taking sensible precautions. Anyone showing several of these in cold, wet, or windy conditions should be treated as hypothermic and warmed and dried immediately rather than watched for another hour. Intense shivering at this stage is a good sign, since it means the body is still generating heat.

As core temperature falls into the moderate range, roughly 90 to 82°F (32 to 28°C), confusion deepens and, counterintuitively, shivering can stop altogether as thermoregulation begins to fail. The absence of shivering in someone who is clearly cold is a serious deterioration, not a sign of recovery. Paradoxical undressing, in which a severely hypothermic person removes clothing because constricted surface vessels suddenly dilate and produce a rush of warmth, appears in this range and is a well-documented finding at cold-weather death scenes. Below about 82°F (28°C) the risks become cardiac arrhythmia and unconsciousness, and a severely hypothermic person can appear dead, with no detectable pulse or breathing, while remaining viable. The working axiom is that nobody is dead until they are warm and dead, and resuscitation should not be abandoned on a cold patient simply because vital signs are hard to find; check breathing and pulse for a full sixty seconds before concluding anything.

Field priority is to stop further heat loss before attempting active rewarming. Get the person out of wind and wet, remove wet clothing, insulate thoroughly from the ground, and wrap them in dry layers with a vapour barrier and a windproof outer shell, the arrangement often called a hypothermia wrap or burrito. Do not rub limbs, do not apply direct high heat to arms and legs, and do not give alcohol; all three drive cold, acidotic blood from the extremities back to the core. Heat packs belong against the chest, armpits, and groin, never directly on skin.

Handle a severely hypothermic person gently. Rough movement can trigger a fatal arrhythmia in a cold heart, a real phenomenon sometimes called rescue collapse, so a cold casualty is moved carefully rather than quickly, and kept horizontal. Warm sweet drinks help only if the person is fully alert and able to swallow reliably.

sections.heading: Gear Worth Carrying for Shelter & Warmth
sections.body:
Most of a good shelter kit is small, cheap, and multi-purpose, bought once and left permanently in a pack. What justifies each item is which of the four heat-loss pathways it addresses, and buying several things that all block the same one is the common mistake.

A metallised emergency blanket is a radiation barrier. Its aluminised surface reflects most of the infrared a body emits, which is genuinely useful for something weighing under two ounces, and it blocks wind. It gives almost no conductive insulation, so it must never be the only thing between you and the ground, and because it is vapour-impermeable, sweat condenses inside it; expect to be damp by morning and treat that as a fair trade. A tarp addresses rain and radiative loss to the sky at once, and unlike a tent it can be pitched a dozen ways to suit the wind. Cordage is what turns a tarp into a shelter.

A closed-cell foam pad is the item most often left behind and most often regretted. It attacks conduction, the largest loss in most improvised shelters, and unlike an inflatable pad it cannot fail from a puncture. A sleeping bag's ratings deserve careful reading: under the ISO standard the comfort rating is what a typical cold sleeper actually needs, while the extreme rating is a six-hour survival figure at which a person is expected to be badly hypothermic rather than asleep. Buy on comfort.

A saw generally beats a hatchet for ridgepoles and ribbing: it cuts faster for the energy spent and is far less likely to open a leg wound in cold, clumsy hands. A wool or synthetic hat and gloves matter out of proportion to their weight, because the head and hands have high surface area, little insulating fat, and, in the hands, the dexterity every other task depends on. A cheap thermometer is the only way to turn a belief that a shelter works into evidence.
ingredients: An emergency space blanket (Mylar), from a camping/outdoor store or pharmacy — reflects radiated body heat back at you; genuinely effective for its size and weight
A lightweight tarp (roughly 8x10 ft, polyester or silnylon, with reinforced corner grommets), from a camping/outdoor or hardware store
50 feet of paracord or similar nylon cordage, from an outdoor/hardware store
A bivy sack, or large heavy-duty contractor-grade trash bags as an improvised rain/wind layer, from an outdoor store or hardware store
A folding saw or small hatchet, from a hardware/outdoor store — for cutting ridge poles and ribbing without exhausting yourself
A closed-cell foam sleeping pad, from a camping store — insulates against ground conduction, which matters more in cold weather than most people expect
A sleeping bag rated comfortably below the coldest temperature you realistically expect, from an outdoor store
A wool or synthetic-fill hat and gloves, from a clothing/outdoor store — the head and extremities lose heat out of proportion to their size
A basic outdoor thermometer, from a hardware or general store — useful for actually testing and proving out shelter insulation, as below

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Sleep-Test a Debris Shelter This Weekend
sections.body: Reading about insulation is not the same as feeling it work, and the gap between the two is where most improvised shelters fail. This exercise turns the physics into a measured result, in conditions where being wrong costs nothing but a cold evening. Two things reliably surprise people on a first attempt: how much debris a roof needs once it compresses, and how much of the night's heat loss went into the ground rather than out through the walls. Both are far easier to learn near a parked car than during an emergency.
steps: In full daylight, pick a site using the terrain criteria above: a bench partway up a slope, not a valley bottom or exposed ridge, checked overhead for dead branches, oriented so the opening faces away from the prevailing wind.
Find or cut a ridgepole a couple of feet longer than your own height, and prop one end on a sturdy forked branch or low tree fork at roughly waist height, with the other end resting on the ground.
Lean ribbing sticks against both sides of the ridgepole at a steep angle, spaced a hand's width apart, to form the shelter's skeleton.
Add a lattice of smaller sticks and twigs crosswise over the ribbing — this is what keeps your insulating debris from sliding straight through the gaps.

Pile debris (dry leaves, pine needles, dry grass, small brush) over the entire structure to a genuine depth of at least 2–3 feet once compressed — this is the single most common failure point of a first attempt: debris that looks thick when loosely piled compresses down to a few insulating inches, so build it far thicker than feels necessary.
Stuff a thick layer of the same dry debris inside the shelter as a sleeping "nest" you'll actually lie on and pull around yourself, since insulation below and around you matters as much as the roof.

Run the test: on a mild-but-cool, dry evening (not your first attempt at genuinely dangerous cold), place one thermometer inside the shelter and a second control thermometer in the open air nearby at the same height, both shielded from direct wind, and compare readings after 30–60 minutes — a well-built shelter typically shows a meaningfully warmer reading, which is your proof the design is working rather than just a guess.

If conditions and preparation allow, sleep-test it for real on a mild night with a backup plan (a car or heated space nearby, someone aware of where you are, and a phone), and use the experience to find and patch drafts, gaps, or thin spots in the debris layer — every real shelter benefits from a second pass once you can feel where the cold is getting in.

Never treat an unverified shelter as your only line of defense in genuinely hazardous cold — build and test in safe, forgiving conditions first, well before you'd ever need to rely on the skill for real.
